disease_name: Acute intermittent porphyria / 急性間欠性ポルフィリン症

distillation_scope.prompt_medical_input: Disease: Acute intermittent porphyria / 急性間欠性ポルフィリン症 (id: D-ACUTE-INTERMITTENT-PORPHYRIA)
distillation_scope.scope_note: Full-spectrum first-layer disease manifold for acute intermittent porphyria. Trigger contexts, cyclic hormonal pattern, recurrent attacks, pregnancy, renal impairment, chronic complications, and treatment safety constraints are represented as context axes, risk factors, or treatment modifiers rather than disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Partial hydroxymethylbilane synthase deficiency creates limited hepatic heme-synthesis reserve. Most carriers remain latent until hepatic ALAS1 induction outstrips downstream pathway capacity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Hepatic ALAS1 induction and heme demand
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Porphyrinogenic medications, fasting or low carbohydrate intake, alcohol, infection, surgery, stress, and hormonal progesterone-dominant states induce hepatic ALAS1 and increase heme demand, initiating an attack in susceptible hosts.

Hepatic ALAS1 induction in HMBS deficiency causes marked accumulation and urinary excretion of delta-aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen. ALA is neurotoxic and oxidative; PBG marks the acute hepatic porphyria biochemical field.

Neurotoxic porphyrin precursors injure autonomic and enteric neural circuits, producing severe abdominal pain without peritonitis, constipation or ileus, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, and urinary retention tendency.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: CNS excitability, psychiatric expression, and SIADH
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Central nervous system involvement from ALA/PBG toxicity, autonomic stress, pain, nausea, and hypothalamic dysregulation produces anxiety, insomnia, agitation, psychosis-like symptoms, delirium, seizure risk, and SIADH-mediated hyponatremia.
Severe or prolonged attacks can injure peripheral motor axons, causing proximal or limb weakness, neuropathic pain, cranial or bulbar weakness, and delayed recovery over weeks to months.
Ascending motor neuropathy, bulbar weakness, severe hyponatremic seizure, oversedation, or aspiration can converge on ventilatory failure and ICU-level mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Recurrent attack and chronic organ stress
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Repeated biochemical attacks and persistent high precursor exposure can leave chronic neuropathic pain, hypertension, kidney injury risk, hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance context, and vulnerability to future attacks.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: AIP is usually caused by heterozygous pathogenic HMBS variants.
Erythrocyte HMBS activity is often reduced in classic AIP, although overlap with normal ranges can occur.
Drugs that induce hepatic heme demand or CYP metabolism can precipitate acute attacks.
Calorie or carbohydrate deprivation derepresses hepatic ALAS1 and can precipitate attacks.
Progesterone-dominant cyclic hormonal exposure is a recognized trigger for attacks in susceptible patients.
Infection, inflammation, surgery, and systemic stress can induce hepatic stress pathways and reduce intake.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: strongest when hepatic ALAS1 induction is active
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Limited HMBS capacity converts ALAS1 induction into precursor accumulation.
ALAS1 induction increases production of ALA and PBG upstream of the deficient HMBS step.
Marked urinary PBG elevation is the key biochemical expression of an acute AIP attack.
ALA rises with hepatic precursor overproduction and contributes to neurotoxicity.
PBG and porphyrin precursor oxidation can darken urine after standing or during high excretion.
Autonomic neuropathy is the most common symptomatic expression of acute precursor neurotoxicity.
Central neurotoxicity, severe pain, nausea, and hypothalamic/autonomic dysfunction contribute to psychiatric symptoms, encephalopathy, and SIADH.
Motor neuropathy usually appears in severe or delayed attacks after sustained precursor neurotoxicity.
Severe diffuse abdominal pain is the dominant clinical presentation of many attacks.
AIP pain is often severe and disproportionate to abdominal examination findings.
Enteric autonomic dysfunction commonly causes constipation.
Severe enteric neuropathy can progress to ileus or pseudo-obstruction physiology.
Sympathetic activation and pain commonly produce tachycardia.
Autonomic excess and pain often raise blood pressure during attacks.
SIADH, nausea, pain, hypotonic fluids, and stress can produce clinically important hyponatremia.
AIP attacks can include SIADH physiology with concentrated urine and low serum sodium.
Hyponatremia and porphyric CNS involvement can cause confusion, delirium, or reduced alertness.
Anxiety, insomnia, agitation, hallucinations, or psychosis-like symptoms can occur during acute attacks.
Hyponatremia and neurotoxicity lower seizure threshold.
AIP neuropathy is usually motor-predominant but can include sensory or pain components.
Motor axonal neuropathy manifests as weakness, often proximal or limb-predominant.
Severe motor neuropathy can involve respiratory muscles.
Bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness moves the disease field toward ventilatory failure.
Respiratory muscle weakness, bulbar dysfunction, aspiration, or seizure can produce acute respiratory failure.
Respiratory failure is a major immediate death pathway in severe AIP.
Seizure, status epilepticus, aspiration, and hypoxic injury increase near-term mortality.
Severe hyponatremia can cause coma, seizure, respiratory compromise, and death.
Recurrent attack history identifies a high-risk disease course and changes preventive-treatment geometry.

supportive_care.care_name: Urgent urine PBG and ALA testing with specimen protection
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Attack confirmation should use urine PBG/ALA rather than nonspecific abdominal pain or psychiatric symptoms alone; treatment should not wait when severe neurologic or respiratory risk is high.
Medication selection can amplify or suppress ALAS1 induction; unsafe anticonvulsants, sedatives, antimicrobials, hormones, and supplements should be treated as context axes.
Motor neuropathy can evolve after pain onset; respiratory failure may be preventable with early monitoring and ventilatory support.
Hyponatremia can be severe and worsened by hypotonic fluids; correction must reduce CNS hazard without overcorrection.
Constipation, vomiting, and poor intake are both symptoms and attack-amplifying contexts through calorie deficit and medication exposure.

supportive_care.care_name: Porphyria specialist follow-up and family counseling
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Long-term care modifies future attack risk, medication safety, renal/liver surveillance, reproductive planning, and family cascade testing.
